summary: Updates DCCP by adding the DCCP-Listen packet, helping applications connect through middleboxes like NATs and when a DCCP server sits behind one. It supports a simultaneous-open technique, in which both ends start the connection at once.

plainLanguage.summary:
Most firewalls and network address translators only let incoming traffic reach a device if that device has recently sent something out. A server hidden behind one of them therefore cannot be reached by a client that has not sent anything first.

This document lets the server send first. The server sends a short message to the client address it expects, which opens the path from its side. The client's own connection request then gets through and the connection is established.

questions: how does dccp work through a nat
what are the dccp invited and listen1 states
subtitle: Lets a DCCP server behind a NAT or firewall reach out first, so both ends can open the connection at once.

tldr.problem: DCCP is connection-oriented, and by default the client sends a request that the server answers. If the server sits behind a NAT or firewall that only lets incoming traffic through after something has been sent out, the client cannot reach it, and a relay server is needed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a new packet type, DCCP-Listen, and two server states. A fully specified server sends DCCP-Listen packets towards the client it expects, which opens the path from the server's side; the client's DCCP-Request then completes the handshake.
tldr.outcome: Connections to a server behind one or more NAPT devices work without a relay, in the cases where a public client reaches a private server and where two private hosts reach each other. The change is interoperable: an implementation that does not support it ignores the new packet.

today: RFC 5596 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates the connection-establishment procedures of RFC 4340 with the DCCP-Listen packet type, assigned the value 10 in the IANA DCCP Packet Types Registry, and it is used with the NAT behaviour described in RFC 5597.

sections.title: The Problem with Asymmetric Roles
sections.content:
The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol is both datagram-based and connection-oriented. In RFC 4340, DCCP servers establish connections by passively listening for incoming connection requests that are actively transmitted by DCCP clients. These asymmetric roles can cause problems when the server is inside a middlebox, such as a Network Address Port Translation device that only allows connection requests to be initiated from inside, for example because of port overloading. Host-based and network firewalls can also implement policies that lead to similar problems, and this behaviour is currently the default for many firewalls.

UDP can support middlebox traversal using techniques that leverage the connectionless nature of UDP, and which are therefore not suitable for DCCP. TCP supports middlebox traversal through the use of its simultaneous-open procedure. The concepts of the TCP solution are applicable to DCCP, but DCCP cannot simply reuse the same methods.

This document specifies an update to the DCCP state machine that offers native support, allowing a DCCP client to establish a connection to a DCCP server that is inside one or more middleboxes. It reduces dependence on external aids such as data relay servers by explicitly supporting a widely used principle known as hole punching. The method requires only a minor change to the standard DCCP operational procedure, and the use of a dedicated DCCP packet type ties usage to a specific condition, which keeps the method interoperable with hosts that do not implement this update or that choose to disable it.
sections.plainLanguage:
DCCP has one side listening and the other side knocking. That works on an open network, but a firewall or a NAT usually refuses traffic that arrives first from outside.

The fix is to let the listening side speak first, in a way that only says it is ready rather than starting the connection.

sections.title: Which Cases Need the Technique
sections.content:
The behavioural requirements for NAT devices supporting DCCP are described in RFC 5597. A traditional NAT that directly maps an IP address to a different IP address does not require the simultaneous-open technique described here.

The method is required when the DCCP server is positioned behind one or more NAPT devices in the path, and hierarchies of nested NAPT devices are possible. DCCP hosts located inside the perimeter controlled by one or more NAPT devices are said to have private addresses, and hosts located in the global address realm are said to have public addresses.

Three scenarios are considered: a private client connecting to a public server, a public client connecting to a private server, and a private client connecting to a private server. A defining characteristic of traditional NAT devices is that private hosts can connect to external hosts but not the other way round, so the first case is possible with the protocol defined in RFC 4340, and a pre-configured static NAT address map would allow outside hosts to establish connections in the other two cases. A DCCP implementation conforming to RFC 4340 together with a NAT device conforming to RFC 5597 would require a DCCP relay server to perform NAT traversal for the second and third cases.

This document describes a method to support those two cases without the aid of a relay server. It updates RFC 4340 and requires the DCCP server to discover the IP address and the DCCP port that correspond to the DCCP client. That signalling may be performed out-of-band, for example using the Session Description Protocol. The technique is relevant to both client/server and peer-to-peer applications, such as Voice over IP, file sharing or online gaming, and it assists connections that use prior out-of-band signalling, for example through a well-known rendezvous server, to notify both endpoints of the connection parameters.
sections.plainLanguage:
The technique is needed when the server is the one behind the translator. If the client is behind it and the server is not, the ordinary request and reply works already.

It also needs the server to learn the client's address in advance, which the two ends normally exchange through a separate signalling exchange, such as the session description used when a call is set up.

sections.title: The DCCP-Listen Packet
sections.content:
The document adds a new DCCP packet type, DCCP-Listen, whose format is that of the DCCP-Request packet with a different Type value. The Source Port field indicates the port on which the DCCP server is listening for a connection from the IP address that appears as the destination IP address in the packet. The Destination Port field indicates the port selected by the DCCP client to identify the connection, and in this technique that value must be communicated out-of-band to the server.

The value of X MUST be set to 1, because a DCCP-Listen packet is sent before a connection is established and there is therefore no way to negotiate the use of short sequence numbers. The value of the Sequence Number field in a DCCP-Listen packet is not related to the DCCP sequence number used in normal DCCP messages. A DCCP server SHOULD set the high and low bits of the Sequence Number field to 0, a DCCP client MUST ignore the value, and middleboxes MUST NOT interpret sequence numbers in DCCP-Listen packets.

The Service Code field contains the service code the server is listening for. It MUST correspond to a service code the server is actually offering for a connection identified by the same source IP address and source port as the DCCP-Listen packet. Because the server may use multiple service codes, the specific value has to be communicated out-of-band from client to server before the DCCP-Listen packet is sent, for example using the Session Description Protocol.

At the time of writing there are no known uses of header options with a DCCP-Listen packet, and clients MUST ignore all options in received DCCP-Listen packets, so feature values cannot be negotiated that way. There are also no known uses of payload data, and because DCCP-Listen packets are issued before a connection is established, endpoints MUST ignore any payload data encountered in them.

Several fields have required values. Data Offset MUST have a value of five or more, that is, at least 20 bytes. CCVal MUST be zero because a connection has not been established. CsCov MUST be zero because use of that feature cannot be negotiated. Type has the value 10, assigned by IANA to denote a DCCP-Listen packet, and X MUST be 1 so that the generic header is used. The remaining fields, including Res and Reserved, are specified by RFC 4340 and its successors, and their interpretation is not modified here.
sections.plainLanguage: The new packet looks like an ordinary DCCP header with a different type number. Three fields carry the meaning: the server's listening port, the port the client has chosen, and the service code. The rest is fixed: the sequence number is ignored and set to zero, the connection counters are zero, and any options or payload are discarded by the receiver.

sections.title: The Server State Machine
sections.content:
Prior to connection setup it is common for a DCCP server endpoint to be not fully specified: before the connection is established, a server usually specifies only the destination port and service code, and sometimes the destination address as well. That leaves the source address and source port unspecified, and the endpoint only becomes fully specified after performing the handshake. For those cases this document does not change RFC 4340, and the server adheres to the existing transitions from CLOSED to LISTEN to RESPOND.

A fully specified server endpoint permits exactly one client, identified by source IP address and port, destination IP address and port and a single service code, to set up the connection. Such a server performs a passive-open from the CLOSED state by inviting the remote client to connect, which is done by sending a single DCCP-Listen packet to the specified remote IP address and port.

Two states are added to those listed in RFC 4340. INVITED is associated with a specific DCCP connection and represents a fully specified server socket in the listening state that is generating DCCP-Listen packets towards the client. LISTEN1 is associated with a specific DCCP connection and represents a fully specified server socket in the passive listening state that will not generate further DCCP-Listen packets towards the client.

The INVITED state is, like LISTEN, a passive state characterised by waiting in the absence of an established connection. If the server in the INVITED state receives a DCCP-Request that matches the set of bound ports and addresses, it transitions to LISTEN1 and then immediately to RESPOND, where further processing resumes as in RFC 4340. If it receives any other packet, the pseudocode generates a DCCP-Reset with the code No Connection, unless the packet was itself a DCCP-Listen, in which case the server may optionally generate a DCCP-Reset with the code Connection Refused, which indicates that two servers are simultaneously awaiting connections on the same port. Server endpoints SHOULD ignore any incoming DCCP-Listen packets.

The server SHOULD repeat sending the DCCP-Listen packet while in the INVITED state, at a 200-millisecond interval with at most 2 repetitions. If the server is still in the INVITED state after a further period of 200ms following transmission of the third DCCP-Listen packet, it SHOULD progress to the LISTEN1 state, where it passively waits for a DCCP-Request. Fully specified server endpoints SHOULD treat ICMP error messages received in response to a DCCP-Listen packet as soft errors that do not cause a state transition, since reception of an ICMP error does not necessarily indicate a failure of the following connection request.
sections.plainLanguage:
The server gains two extra steps. In the first, it has sent its signal and is waiting to see whether the client responds. In the second, it has stopped sending signals and is simply waiting for the client's connection request. When the request arrives, the server replies and the handshake continues as before.

The signal is sent up to three times, 200 milliseconds apart, so that a lost copy does not lose the connection.

sections.title: An Example Exchange
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, DCCP A is the client and DCCP B is the server. A middlebox NA is placed before DCCP A and another middlebox NB before DCCP B, and both use a policy that permits DCCP packets to traverse the device for outgoing links but only permits incoming DCCP packets when a previous packet has been sent out for the same connection.

DCCP A and DCCP B decide to communicate using an out-of-band mechanism, labelled SDP in the figure, whereupon the client and server are started. DCCP B actively indicates its listening state by sending a DCCP-Listen message. This fulfills the requirement of punching a hole in NB, and creates the binding to the external address and port. The message is dropped by NA, since no hole exists there yet. DCCP A initiates a connection by entering the REQUEST state and sending a DCCP-Request, which, if NA were a NAT device, would also result in a binding that maps the pinhole to the external address and port. The DCCP-Request is received by DCCP B through the binding at NB. DCCP B transmits the DCCP-Response and the connection is established through the bindings now in place at NA and NB.

Repetition covers the case where the request does not arrive. The timer is restarted with an interval of 200ms when sending each DCCP-Listen packet and is cancelled when the server leaves the INVITED state. If it expires after the first and second transmission it triggers another DCCP-Listen packet, and if it expires after the third, the server enters LISTEN1 and waits for a DCCP-Request.

An optional client optimisation avoids waiting for a timeout after a dropped DCCP-Request. A client that implements it MAY immediately retransmit a DCCP-Request after receiving the first DCCP-Listen packet, in the same manner as a timeout in the REQUEST state, and the retransmission SHOULD result in the client increasing the exponential-backoff timer interval. Because a path delay greater than 200ms will result in multiple DCCP-Listen packets arriving before a DCCP-Response is received, clients MUST perform only one such retransmission for each connection, which requires maintaining local state such as one flag per connection. Host timing or path reordering can result in the server receiving two DCCP-Requests and the client sending a second, unnecessary DCCP-Response; these additional packets are not expected to modify or delay the open procedure.
sections.plainLanguage:
The server's signal opens the path from the server's side of the translator. The client's request opens the path from the client's side. Once both sides have sent something, the packets can flow in both directions and the handshake finishes.

Because a signal can be lost, it is repeated three times. As an optional extra, a client that receives the signal can immediately resend its request instead of waiting for its own timer to expire.

sections.title: Compatibility with RFC 4340
sections.content:
No changes are required if a DCCP client conforming to this document communicates with a DCCP server conforming to RFC 4340. If a client implements only RFC 4340, an incoming DCCP-Listen packet would be ignored because of the first step in Section 8.1 of RFC 4340, which at the same time also conforms to the behaviour specified by this document.

This document further does not modify communication for any DCCP server that implements a passive-open without fully binding the addresses, ports and service codes to be used. The authors therefore do not expect practical deployment problems with existing conformant DCCP implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that has never heard of this update ignores the new packet, so a new client and an old server still work. And a server that does not know the client's address in advance behaves exactly as before.

sections.title: Why a New Packet Type
sections.content:
The DCCP-Listen packet has the same format as the DCCP-Request packet, and the only difference is in the value of the Type field. The usage differs: the DCCP-Listen packet serves as an advisory message, not as part of the actual connection setup, so sequence numbers have no meaning and no payload can be communicated.

A DCCP-Request packet could in theory have been used for the same purpose, but the RFC gives three reasons against it. The first is semantic overloading: the DCCP-Request serves a well-defined purpose as the initial packet of the three-way handshake, and using it for another purpose would require DCCP processors to have two different processing paths, which would complicate packet processing in hosts and in particular in stateful middleboxes, which may have restricted computational resources.

The second problem is that a client receiving a DCCP-Request from a server could generate a DCCP-Reset packet if it had not yet entered the REQUEST state. The method in this document lets client endpoints ignore DCCP-Listen packets; adding a similar rule for DCCP-Request would have been cumbersome, because clients would not have been able to distinguish between a DCCP-Request meant to indicate an intention to accept a new connection and a genuinely erratic connection initiation.

The third problem is similar and refers to a client receiving the indication after having itself sent a connection-initiation DCCP-Request. RFC 4340 requires the client to reply to a DCCP-Request from the server with a DCCP-Sync packet, and since sequence numbers are ignored for this type of message, additional and complex processing would be necessary. Using a separate packet type allows simpler and clearer processing.

The sequence number fields were retained in the DCCP-Listen header only to reuse the generic header format. The rationale for ignoring them is that the endpoints have not yet entered connection setup: the DCCP-Listen packet is sent while the server is still in the passive-open INVITED state, and it has not yet allocated state other than binding to the client's IP address and port and service code.

A DCCP server should by default permit generation of DCCP-Listen packets. Since these packets solve a particular problem with NAT and firewall traversal, their generation on passive sockets is tied to the condition that the remote address and service code are both known in advance, so that it does not interfere with normal DCCP connections where client addresses are generally not known in advance. Repetition is a necessary requirement to increase robustness when a DCCP-Listen packet is lost due to congestion, link loss or some other reason. The maximum of three timeouts, that is two repeated copies, was chosen because the repeated copies need to be spaced far enough apart to avoid correlated loss, and the 200ms interval accommodates a wide range of wireless and wired paths. The DCCP-Request retransmission interval of one second is the other constraint: intermediate systems need to receive a DCCP-Listen packet before the request times out, and three timeouts spaced 200 milliseconds apart still come to 600 milliseconds, below one second and long enough to allow for longer one-way delays as on some wireless links.
sections.plainLanguage:
The new packet could have been an ordinary connection request with a flag set, but the RFC explains why a separate type is cleaner. A request already has a meaning in the handshake, and reusing it would force every router and firewall to work out which of two meanings applies, doubling the processing in devices that have little to spare.

The repetition rules are set by two numbers: the client waits one second before retrying its request, so the server has to send its signal three times at 200 millisecond intervals to fit inside that window.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General security considerations for DCCP are described in RFC 4340, and security considerations for service codes are further described in RFC 5595.

The method generates a DCCP-Listen packet addressed to a specific DCCP client. This exposes the state of a DCCP server that is in a passive listening state, waiting to accept a connection from a known client. The exposed information is not encrypted and could be seen on the network path to the DCCP client. An attacker on this return path could observe a DCCP-Listen packet and then exploit this by spoofing a packet, such as a DCCP-Request or DCCP-Reset, with the IP addresses, DCCP ports and service code that correspond to the values to be used for the connection. As in other on-path attacks, this could be used to inject data into a connection or to deny a connection request. A similar on-path attack is also possible for any DCCP connection once the session is initiated by the client.

The DCCP-Listen packet is only sent in response to explicit, prior out-of-band signalling from the client to the server, and will normally directly precede a DCCP-Request sent by the client, which carries the same information. The update does not significantly increase the complexity or vulnerability of a DCCP implementation that conforms to RFC 4340, so a server SHOULD by default permit generation of DCCP-Listen packets. A server that wishes to prevent disclosing this information MAY refrain from generating them, without impacting subsequent DCCP state transitions but possibly inhibiting middlebox traversal.

The DCCP base specification defines an Init Cookie option, which lets a DCCP server avoid having to hold any state until the three-way connection-setup handshake has completed. This specification enables an out-of-band mechanism that forces the server to hold state for a connection that has not yet been established. This is a change in the security profile of DCCP, although the impact is expected to be minimal and depends on the security features of the out-of-band mechanism, and SIP SDP is one such mechanism that provides sufficient security features.

The method creates a new way for a client to set up a DCCP connection to a server using out-of-band data transported over a signalling connection. If that signalling connection is not encrypted, an eavesdropper could see the client IP address and the port for the to-be-established connection, and generate a DCCP-Listen packet towards the client using its own server IP address and port. However, a client will only respond to a received DCCP-Listen packet if the server IP address and port match an existing DCCP connection that is in the REQUEST state, so the method cannot be used to redirect the connection to a different server IP address.
sections.plainLanguage:
The signal reveals that a server is waiting for a particular client, and it is not encrypted. An attacker on the path could see it and try to send a forged packet with the same addresses, which could inject data into the connection or block it.

The method also means the server has to hold state for a connection that has not started yet, where the base protocol would have waited until the handshake began. That is a small change in the security profile, and it depends on how well the out-of-band signalling that told the server the client's address was protected.
